rows.title: What’s Working: Lesser-known Colorado agriculture programs are feeling the federal funding freeze too
rows.standfirst: It’s not just U.S. park and forestry workers. Plus: SBA may move out of Denver office, tipped-workers protest changes to tipped wages, more!

rows.title: Colorado School of Mines project hopes to warm houses, lower bills in mobile home communities
rows.standfirst: The goal of the three-year program is to bring energy efficiency to low-income families and communities. “It’s a big difference,” one resident says.

rows.title: Surprise rental fees, impostor fraud are fastest risers in Colorado AG’s list of consumer complaints in 2024
rows.standfirst: Unauthorized subscriptions contribute to the top category of consumer complaints but others rose faster.

rows.title: Home improvements help people age independently. But Medicare seldom picks up the bill.
rows.standfirst: Community Aging in Place: Advancing Better Living for Elders, or CAPABLE, has been around for 15 years and is offered in about 65 places across 26 states, including Colorado.

rows.title: Supporters of Colorado tipped minimum wage bill say their businesses are being “harassed” with angry calls, hostile reviews
rows.standfirst: Some restaurant owners who had previously signed up to speak out at the Capitol in support of the bill are now having second thoughts

rows.title: Trump’s tariffs are estimated to cost Colorado $1.4 billion a year. Consumers could feel the pain soon.
rows.standfirst: Hours after new 10% to 25% tariffs on imports from China, Mexico and Canada began, small business owners wondered how they’re going to cover the tax hike

rows.title: Grand County ranchers will receive almost $350,000 in compensation for animals lost to wolves last year
rows.standfirst: “This is not a bonus. It is trying to recover some costs that have been lost and should have been paid to these producers last fall,” Colorado Wildlife Commission chair Dallas May says

rows.title: U.S. Small Business Administration is moving out of Denver because it’s a “sanctuary city”
rows.standfirst: Under new management, the small business agency is also exiting five other U.S. cities in the coming months. SBA officials did not share what city the Denver office will move to.

rows.title: What’s Working: Trump’s tariff roller coaster is no fun for Colorado’s farm and agriculture industry
rows.standfirst: Plus: Colorado’s top imports and exports that face tariffs, consumer-protection week tips, moon landing goes sideways, and more!

rows.title: Is Denver’s tipped minimum wage $4 higher than its surrounding area?
rows.standfirst: Yes. The tipped minimum wage in Denver is $15.79, compared with the state minimum of $11.79, which applies in most nearby cities and towns.

rows.title: PHOTOS: The Colorado sheep shearers who help fuel the fashion world
rows.standfirst: Photojournalist William Woody captures sheep shearers hard at work at a Colorado ranch ahead of lambing season

rows.title: Bags will no longer fly free on Southwest Airlines
rows.standfirst: Southwest says people who haven’t either reached the upper tiers of its Rapid Rewards loyalty program, bought a business class ticket or hold the airline’s credit card will have to pay for checked bags

rows.title: Is natural gas a bridge to clean energy or a climate backslide? That’s a Colorado power company’s dilemma.
rows.standfirst: The Platte River Power Authority wants to install five natural gas turbines to ease its transition into renewables, but local residents and state lawmakers don’t want to go backward

rows.title: Black Hills Energy allowed to raise electric bills by $17M for 309,000 southern Colorado customers
rows.standfirst: That’s much less than the $37 million rate increase the utility had sought, but consumer advocates argued Black Hills should have received no increase at all

rows.title: 608 federal workers have filed for unemployment in Colorado — so far — as Trump cuts continue
rows.standfirst: The state’s labor department expects “a continuing increase” in new claims from fired federal workers

rows.title: What’s Working: Colorado’s tipped minimum wage would be left up to local governments under bill compromise
rows.standfirst: The amended bill passed another stage that has no side pleased but could provide some relief to restaurants, especially in Denver. Plus: Same data, different conclusions, and what’s a fired federal worker to do?

rows.title: A big house in Grand Junction, now home to 20 troubled men, tests Colorado’s new affordable housing law
rows.standfirst: The owner of Rene’s House says the men merely choose to live together. But Bookcliff Heights residents say their new neighbors are referred by the criminal justice system.

rows.title: Douglas County loses bid to revive its creative $28 million property tax relief plan
rows.standfirst: Denver District Court Judge Ericka F. H. Englert ruled that the State Board of Equalization’s decision was “properly considered” and thus valid. The bulk of Douglas County’s lawsuit was rejected last year

rows.title: Mountain Village condemns land owned by Telluride ski resort’s erratic owner, revealing decades of frustration
rows.standfirst: The rift over permission to use Chuck Horning’s parcel for a 25-year-old summer concert series marks a rare public exposure of long-simmering concerns with a temperamental resort owner who has fired many managers

rows.title: Are more restaurants closing or opening in Denver? Here’s what we found in the data.
rows.standfirst: There is always more to the data. We wanted to see what “more” there was. Here are the sources, what they say and what they mean.

rows.title: Colorado would become second state to limit when workers can be fired under union-backed ballot measure
rows.standfirst: Initiative 43 would prohibit companies with more than eight employees from firing or suspending a worker without so-called just cause

rows.title: Former Wyoming legislator Cyrus Western picked to run EPA Region 8 office in Denver
rows.standfirst: New regional EPA administrator says it is his honor to implement President Trump’s “pro-energy, pro-middle class agenda.” Supporters say cuts to the agency will make the task difficult.

rows.title: Does the average Denver restaurant server make less than $40,000 a year?
rows.standfirst: Yes. Waiters and waitresses in the Denver metropolitan area make an average of $39,170 annually, labor data shows.

rows.title: Colorado’s unemployment rate was worse than previously thought in every month last year
rows.standfirst: Why did that happen? With new and better data coming in, preliminary results were revised to a 4.3% unemployment rate in 2024, instead of 3.9%. In January, the new jobless rate hit 4.7%.

rows.title: Pueblo museum featuring Leonardo da Vinci inventions will be the first of its kind in North America
rows.standfirst: As Professional Bull Riding says goodbye to downtown, a new collection of authentically reconstructed da Vinci contraptions says hello.

rows.title: Who will squash the bracket in Colorado State’s second annual Veggie Madness tournament?
rows.standfirst: It came down to potatoes vs. winter squash in Colorado State University’s Veggie Madness, a friendly rivalry between CSU extension offices

rows.title: What’s Working: How some rural Colorado businesses tapped an unheralded state resource and reaped financial returns
rows.standfirst: One ended up on HGTV. Another saw customers triple. Plus: Colorado overestimated its job growth in 2024, restaurant bills (the law-making kind) and more!

rows.title: License applications pour in as Colorado prepares for psychedelic healing centers to open in late spring
rows.standfirst: At least 15 healing centers are seeking licenses, as are 9 cultivators of psilocybin, 4 manufacturers and 1 testing facility.

rows.title: Colorado overcharged businesses $5 million for unemployment insurance last year. It’s getting refunded.
rows.standfirst: Adjustments to the state’s unemployment technology are still underway with refunds expected this summer. State auditors also found issues with Colorado’s paid-family leave program, FAMLI.

rows.title: Growing government workers union holds rally outside of EPA’s downtown Denver offices
rows.standfirst: The American Federation of Government Employees, the largest union of federal workers in the nation, is organizing protests and filing lawsuits to keep federal workers in their jobs

rows.title: Plan to change Colorado Flight for Life helicopters’ color has many seeing red
rows.standfirst: The health care provider plans to change its emergency vehicle livery from orange to purple, sparking outrage among Flight for Life vets who would rather see investment in safety, not marketing.

rows.title: What’s Working: Denver chamber winds down diversity tool that just didn’t do the job
rows.standfirst: The hope was to move low-paid workers into higher paid jobs and careers as a business community. But sharing demographic data had privacy challenges. Plus: Colorado lost jobs in February, unemployment rate stayed the same, and more!

rows.title: Is Denver Health mostly funded through taxpayer dollars?
rows.standfirst: Yes. Nearly 60% of Denver Health’s $1.5 billion in revenue comes from public funding through Medicare and Medicaid.

rows.title: Why there are a growing number of unsellable condos in Colorado
rows.standfirst: Many HOAs hoping to limit a spike in monthly condo fees are opting for higher deductibles, more deferred maintenance. They may not be aware that those decisions may prevent buyers from getting a conventional loan.

rows.title: Many states require porn sites to verify their users’ age. Colorado may be next.
rows.standfirst: Senate Bill 201 would require pornographic websites that are accessible in Colorado to verify their users are at least 18 years old, either by sharing photo ID or through photos screened by artificial intelligence. The governor is skeptical.
